claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is primarily governed by engineered multilayer interfaces.
Engineered multilayer interfaces increase the nucleation barrier for partial dislocations.
Delaying partial-dislocation nucleation delays stacking-fault formation.
Partial-dislocation activity and resulting stacking faults contribute to plastic deformation under loading.
CoCrFeMnNi can be an equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
The proposed initial coating has a multilayer structure with sharp coherent or incoherent interfaces.
Alternating compositionally identical or similar HEA layers introduces engineered multilayer interfaces.
Engineered multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation nucleation and motion.
Interfaces disrupt continuous slip paths in multilayer HEA coatings.
Multilayer interfaces raise the stress required to nucleate partial dislocations relative to homogeneous monolithic coatings.
Partial dislocations can nucleate from twist grain boundaries in equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi at 77 K, bow into the bulk during further loading, and leave stacking faults.
The behavior of multilayer interfaces is mechanistically similar to that of twist grain boundaries.
Under equivalent sustained loading, multilayer coatings will accumulate less time-dependent plastic strain than monolithic coatings of the same overall composition.
Multilayer coatings will have improved creep resistance relative to monolithic coatings.
Multilayer coatings will have a higher yield point than monolithic coatings.
The proposed mechanism is most applicable when multilayer interfaces are well-defined and coherent.
Layers that are too thin may interdiffuse and diminish the interface-mediated effect.
Elevated temperatures may diminish the effect through interface instability or diffusion.
